introduction: On this Sunday after Christmas we celebrate the Holy Family of Jesus, Mary and Joseph. The readings speak of faith tested and rewarded: Abraham trusted God's promise of a son, and in the Temple the elderly Simeon and Anna recognise the child Jesus as the salvation of God. As we celebrate, let us pray for our own families, with their joys and struggles, and ask the Holy Family to watch over them.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Through the intercession of Jesus, Mary and Joseph, let us bring the needs of all families before God.
intentions: For the Church, the family of God: that she may support and strengthen families in every land. Let us pray to the Lord.
For families living through poverty, illness, migration or conflict: that they may find help and keep hope. Let us pray to the Lord.
For married couples, and for those preparing for marriage: that they may grow in faithful and generous love. Let us pray to the Lord.
For the elderly, especially those who are lonely or forgotten: that, like Simeon and Anna, they may know they have a place in God's plan. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our own families: that our homes may be places of prayer, forgiveness and joy. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: God our Father, you gave your Son a home in the family of Nazareth. Hear our prayers, and bless all families with your peace. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Faith in an ordinary home
reflection.body:
The Holy Family can seem far removed from our own. Their child is the Son of God; Mary is without sin; Joseph is a saint. Our homes are messier. Yet today's readings show a family whose life was shaped not by perfection but by faith, often in hard circumstances.

The first reading tells of Abraham and Sarah, old and childless, who had waited years for God's promise. God leads Abram outside: "Look now toward the sky, and count the stars." So many will be his descendants. Then comes a line that Paul will quote centuries later: "He believed in the LORD, who credited it to him for righteousness." The Letter to the Hebrews praises the same trust: "By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went."

Mary and Joseph lived by that same faith. In the Gospel they bring the infant Jesus to the Temple to fulfil the law. They are poor; their offering is two birds, the gift allowed to those who could not afford a lamb. There they meet two elderly people who have spent their lives waiting. Simeon takes the child in his arms and prays, "for my eyes have seen your salvation." Anna, a widow who has prayed in the Temple for decades, begins to speak about the child to everyone who is waiting for redemption.

Simeon also tells Mary something hard: "a sword will pierce through your own soul." The Holy Family will know exile, misunderstanding and finally the cross. Their holiness did not spare them suffering; it carried them through it.

Our families, too, are places where faith is tested. Children grow and leave, parents age and need care, misunderstandings wound. The Gospel ends simply: "The child was growing, and was becoming strong in spirit, being filled with wisdom." That is the work of every Christian home: to make room for God's grace to grow.
